content.explanation: Arabic nouns are either definite or indefinite. The definite article is ال (al-). When attached, it changes based on the first letter of the noun—sun letters cause assimilation, moon letters keep the ل sound.

examples.rule: Sun letter — ال assimilates and the ش takes a shadda
Moon letter — ال keeps its ل sound

rules.name: Sun Letters (حروف شمسية)
rules.description: When ال attaches to a noun starting with one of these letters, the ل is dropped and the following letter takes a shadda
rules.letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن

rules.name: Moon Letters (حروف قمرية)
rules.description: When ال attaches to a noun starting with one of these letters, the ل is pronounced
rules.letters: ا ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي

exercises.question: Which of these is a moon letter?
exercises.explanation: ب is a moon letter. ت، س، and ر are sun letters.

exercises.question: Complete: ال + كِتَاب = ___
exercises.explanation: ك is a moon letter, so the ل is pronounced.

content.explanation: Arabic verbs change based on the subject. The past tense (ماضي) is the simplest form — add suffixes to the root to indicate who performed the action.

exercises.question: Match the conjugation of كَتَبَ (he wrote) with the correct subject

content.explanation: Arabic sentences begin with either a noun (nominal sentence / جملة اسمية) or a verb (verbal sentence / جملة فعلية). A nominal sentence has two parts: the subject (مبتدأ) and the predicate (خبر).

exercises.question: Identify the مبتدأ (subject) in: الْبَابُ مَسْدُودٌ
exercises.explanation: الْبَابُ is the مبتدأ (subject/noun that begins the sentence).

content.explanation: The present tense (مضارع) is formed by adding prefixes to the verb root. The prefix indicates the subject: أ (I), ت (you/he/she), ي (he/she), ن (we).

exercises.question: Complete: يَكْتُبُ → they (men) write = ___
exercises.explanation: The plural masculine suffix is وُنا for present tense.

content.explanation: Arabic nouns change their ending based on their grammatical role in the sentence. This is called i'rab (إعراب). The three cases are: nominative (مرفوع) with ـُ, accusative (منصوب) with ـَ, genitive (مجرور) with ـِ.

exercises.question: What case ending does the subject of a sentence take?
exercises.explanation: The subject (فاعل) takes the nominative case with damma (ـُ).

content.explanation: Arabic expresses possession by placing two nouns together rather than using a word for “of”. The first noun (المضاف) takes no article and carries whatever case its role in the sentence requires. The second (المضاف إليه) is always genitive. So رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ is “Lord of the worlds” — two nouns, no connecting word.

examples.rule: المضاف takes no article; المضاف إليه is genitive
Both nouns genitive here, because the phrase follows مَٰلِكِ

rules.name: The first term (المضاف)
rules.description: Never carries ال and never carries tanween. Its case is set by its role in the wider sentence.

rules.name: The second term (المضاف إليه)
rules.description: Always genitive (مجرور), whatever the sentence around it is doing.

exercises.question: In رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ, what case is ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ?
exercises.explanation: The second term of an idafa is always genitive.

exercises.question: Which is NOT allowed on the first term of an idafa?
exercises.explanation: المضاف never takes ال. That is how you recognise the construction.

content.explanation: Arabic attaches pronouns directly to the end of nouns, verbs and prepositions rather than writing them separately. On a noun the pronoun means possession; on a verb it is the object; on a preposition it is what the preposition governs. The same ending does all three jobs, so context decides.

examples.rule: The isolated object pronoun, used to front the object
The نـ prefix carries “we”, so no separate pronoun is needed

rules.name: On a noun — possession
rules.description: كِتَابُهُ means “his book”. The ـهُ is the possessor.

rules.name: On a verb — object
rules.description: The same ـهُ attached to a verb is the thing acted upon, not the actor.

exercises.question: Attached to a noun, what does an attached pronoun express?
exercises.explanation: On a noun it marks the possessor.

content.explanation: Almost every Arabic word is built from a three-letter root poured into a pattern. The pattern changes the meaning in a regular way: Form I is the plain action, Form II often intensifies or makes it causative, Form III makes it mutual, Form IV makes it causative. Learn the patterns and one root gives you a family of words.

examples.rule: Form IV of ن ز ل — causative
Form II of the same root — intensive or repeated

rules.name: Form I (فَعَلَ)
rules.description: The bare root. The corpus marks Forms II–XII and leaves this one unmarked, because Form I IS the plain triliteral.

rules.name: Form IV (أَفْعَلَ)
rules.description: Prefixes أ and makes the action causative: to cause something to happen.

exercises.question: أَنزَلَ and نَزَّلَ share a root. What differs?
options: The derived form, and so the shade of meaning
exercises.explanation: أَنزَلَ is Form IV and نَزَّلَ is Form II. Same root ن ز ل, different pattern.

exercises.question: Why does the corpus not label Form I explicitly?
options: Form I is the bare root, so an absent marker means Form I
exercises.explanation: An unmarked verb is Form I. Reading that as “unknown” would drop the commonest form entirely.

content.explanation: Arabic demonstratives agree with what they point at in gender and number, and distinguish near from far. When a demonstrative is followed by a noun carrying ال, the two together form a single phrase — “this book” — rather than a sentence.

rules.name: Near vs far
rules.description: هَٰذَا points at what is close; ذَٰلِكَ at what is distant, in space or in the discourse.

rules.name: With a definite noun
rules.description: ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ is “that book” — a phrase. Without ال it would read as a full sentence.

exercises.question: Which points at something near?
exercises.explanation: هَٰذَا is the near masculine singular; ذَٰلِكَ is its far counterpart.

content.explanation: Arabic negates with different particles depending on what is being negated and when. لَا negates a present-tense verb or, in another use, negates a category outright. مَا negates a past-tense verb. لَنْ negates the future and puts the verb in the subjunctive. Choosing the wrong particle changes the tense, not just the tone.

examples.rule: Negates the present, or negates a category absolutely
Negates the past tense — also serves as “what” elsewhere

rules.name: لَا with the present
rules.description: لَا يَعْلَمُ — “he does not know”. The verb stays indicative.

rules.name: مَا with the past
rules.description: مَا قَالَ — “he did not say”. The verb keeps its past form.

exercises.question: Which particle negates a past-tense verb?
exercises.explanation: مَا negates the past. لَا handles the present and لَنْ the future.

exercises.question: What does لَنْ do besides negate?
options: Puts the verb in the subjunctive
exercises.explanation: لَنْ negates the future and governs the subjunctive.
